title: The good shepherd (John 10:11–18)
hookLine: he knows his sheep and lays down his life

cards: Go down into the catacombs under Rome, the underground burial passages of the early Christians, and look at the painted walls.
Long before the cross became the most common Christian image, one picture shows up again and again: a young man with a sheep across his shoulders, holding its legs in front of his chest.

Some of these paintings go back to the two hundreds, the third century. When the first Christians wanted to picture Jesus near the graves of the people they loved, many of them chose this. It comes from today's words.

teach.b: "I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep." This is the fourth I am saying in John, right on the heels of the door. The word for good is kalos: good, and also beautiful, noble.
The shepherd as he ought to be. Jesus sets him beside the hired hand.
The hireling, as the King James calls him, sees a wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and runs. Not because he's evil. Because they're not his sheep; he's paid by the day.
The good shepherd stays, because they're his own. Then a line of real tenderness: "I am the good shepherd, and know my sheep, and am known of mine."
Knowing goes both ways. Shepherd pictures run deep in the scriptures Jesus grew up with. King David was a shepherd.
Psalm twenty-three begins, the Lord is my shepherd. In Ezekiel, God condemns shepherds who feed themselves instead of the flock, and promises to search for the lost sheep himself.

teach.h: OTHER SHEEP, NOT OF THIS FOLD.
teach.b: Jesus steps into that old picture, and adds: "And other sheep I have, which are not of this fold." Christians have long read that as a sign the flock would grow wider than anyone listening expected.
And the most striking part: no one takes his life from him.

teach.h: I LAY IT DOWN OF MYSELF.
teach.b: "I lay it down of myself." The good shepherd isn't caught off guard. He chooses to give his life for the sheep, freely.

how: Many churches keep a Good Shepherd Sunday in the Easter season, and the image of Christ carrying a sheep remains common in stained glass, children's Bibles and church art.

o: a thief who climbs over the fold's wall

games.q: what's inside John 10:11–18 — tap the pairs.
p: no one takes it from me

s: the good shepherd with a sheep is one of the oldest images of Jesus
it appears in Roman catacombs as early as the third century.
the hireling runs because he's evil
he runs because the sheep aren't his own; he's paid by the day.
Jesus says his life will be taken from him
"no man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself."

games.q: you're watching the flock for pay. a wolf comes over the hill. what does the hireling in the story do?
games.why: the hireling flees, because the sheep aren't his. the good shepherd stays and gives his life for them.

practice: Think of the people you see often but don't really know, the person at the coffee shop, a neighbor, someone at work you nod to, and pick one whose name you know or would like to learn, and picture saying it to them warmly.

Then remember a time someone used your name when you didn't expect them to know it, and how that felt. If you pray, give thanks that you're known by name; if not, just hold the feeling of being known.

wordCard.voice: Hireling. The hired hand who runs when the wolf comes, because the sheep aren't his own, unlike the good shepherd who stays and lays down his life.
